topics.title: Compilation of Factoring Tricks
topics.text:
Hey,



I was thinking that we can compile some factoring tricks? (Sophie German, difference of squares, cubes, SFFT, etc.)



Just put the trick (and please make sure its a unique one). I'll start, and I'll update this OP with new tricks that people put.



5 tricks1. $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$ - Difference of Squares

2. $a^4+4b^4= (a^2+2b^2+2ab)(a^2+2b^2-2ab)$ - Sophie German

3. $(x-1)(y-1)=xy-x-y+1$ $(x+1)(y+1) = xy+x+y+1$ SFFT: Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick (Take a common factor out of the expressions and add a constant

4. $(a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} a^{n - k} b^k$ - Binomial Theorem

5. $x^3 \pm y^3 = (x \pm y)(x^2 \mp xy + y^2)$ - Sum/Difference of cubes




Keep it going!

topics.title: Preparation Contest!
topics.text:
Hello AoPS!

Because MATHCOUNTS and other competitions are coming soon, merelephant and I have decided to create a contest to help you prepare. There will be three rounds, and more rounds as well as a team round if a lot of people sign up. Each round will consist of 10 problems. The first round will be on 2/7. You will have 8 to 10 days for each round. I will post the results for each round, and the final results when the competition is over. I will also post the answer key. If you prefer your scores to be private, put a * after your name when you sign up.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Round 1 is weighted 1 in your final score. (1/6 of it)

Round 2 is weighted 2 in your final score. (1/3 of it)

Round 3 is weighted 3 in your final score. (1/2 of it)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To sign up, use this format;

Signups(number of people)1. username

2. username

......


Quote the person above you and then remove the quotes. Signups are perpetually open.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If you have any questions, feel free to ask.

Thanks for signing up!

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ROUND 1Problem 1: In circle $O$, radius $OA$ bisects chord $CH$ at point $B$. If $OB = 4$ and $CH = 6$, then what is the length of segment $BA$?



Problem 2: $X$ is an integer whose digits are all 1's and 0's and has at least one 1 and one 0. If $x$ is divisible by 9, what is the least possible value of $x$?



Problem 3:  A dogs leash is tied to the corner of a shop. If the shop is a cube with side length $6$ feet, and the leash is $8$ feet long, what is the area of the ground that the dog can stand on? Assume that the dog can be only where his leash can reach, and that the dog is outside of the shop and cannot enter the shop. Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.



Problem 4: How many factors does 100,000,000,000,000 have, including 1 and itself?



Problem 5: How many one, two or three digit numbers contain a 3, 4, or a 5 but not more than one of those three numbers? (For example, 382 and 940 work, but 336 and 340 do not.)



Problem 6: A family has three children, all of whom are either a boy or a girl. Two of the kids are boys. (Consider the boys identical). What is the probability that the third child is a girl? Answer as a common fraction.



Problem 7: How many positive integers $(a, b, c)$ satisfy $a^2 + 2ab + 2ac + b^2 + 2bc + c^2 = 900$?



Problem 8: A prison guard has to divide a certain amount of prisoners into jail cells. When he divides the prisoners into groups of 2, he has 1 left over. When he divides them into groups of 3, he has 2 left over. When he divides them into groups of 4, he has 3 left over. When he divides them into groups of 5, he has 4 left over. When he divides them into groups of 6, he has 5 left over. When he divides them into groups of 7, he has 6 left over. When he divides them into groups of 8, he has 7 left over. When he divides them into groups of 9, he has 8 left over. When he divides them into groups of 10, he has 9 left over. When he divides them into groups of 11, there are none left over. What is the smallest positive number of prisoners the guard could have?



Problem 9: What is the smallest positive integer greater than one that is a perfect square, cube, and fourth power?



Problem 10: At a party, there were only families with one kid and families with two kids. If the kids all shook hands with all of the other kids except for their siblings, there were $20$ kids in total and $182$ total handshakes, how many single kids were there?

ROUND 2!Problem 1$$a<b<c\quad a,b,c \in \mathbb{R}$$$$a+3b-4c=-3$$$$4ac+12bc-3ab=6$$$$3abc=-2$$$$\text{Find }a+b+c.$$




Problem 2A pair of scissors is made up of several shapes (all measurements are in centimeters)

- two circles of radius $5$ with a hole inside each with radius $4$

- an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with side lengths of $AB=AC=13$ and $BC=10$

The two circles are tangent to each other at point $O$, and the points $B$ and $C$ are each on a different circle.

The figure $BCO$, made up of two circle segments and a line, is also a part of the pair of scissors.



If $20$ foot tall tree on a hill gives a shadow of length $40$ feet, then the area, in square centimeters, of the shadow of the scissors when placed vertically on the same slope can be expressed in the form $a+b\pi$. Find $a+b$. Assume that the tree and the scissors are both perpendicular to the ground.




Problem 3In Infinity town, there is an infinite number of people. The people love girls. Every family continues to have children until they have a girl, at which point they stop having kids. Hence, the orders in which couples have kids are limited to:

G

BG

BBG

BBBG

BBBBBG

etc...

What is the probability that a randomly selected child is a boy? Assume that all of the kids in Infinity town are either boys or girls. Express your answer as a common fraction.




Problem 4In $\triangle ABC$, points $D,E$, and $F$ lie on $BC,AC$, and $AB$ respectively such that $AD,BE,CF$ intersect at a common point $G$. If $AE:EC=2:5$ and $AF:FB=8:17$, then the value of $\frac{AG}{GD}\cdot\frac{BG}{GE}\cdot\frac{CG}{GF}$ can be expressed as $\frac{m}{n}$ for relatively prime positive integers $m,n$. Find $m+n$.




Problem 5Macy is making shapes out of sticks. She has one stick of length $5$ feet, $7$ feet, $12$ feet, and $18$ feet. To make a polygon, she puts the ends of the sticks together (all of the endpoints of the sticks must touch), and she can combine two sticks to form a longer stick (she can put the $5$ and the $7$ foot long sticks together to create another stick of length $12$). How many distinct convex polygons can she make?



Edit to question 5: Polygons are considered unique if they cannot be rotated or reflected to obtain another polygon. For example, a polygon ABCD would be the same thing as BCDA, but not the same thing as ABDC. She only has one of each length of stick, and you don't have to use all of them.




Problem 6In a park, there are trees and a dog. If the park were a coordinate grid, the following would be true:

The dog's $8$ foot long leash is tied to the tree at point $(0,0)$

There are $7$ trees at points $(8,0),(3,4),(0,4),(2,4),(3,0),(7,3),(4,0)$.

The dog can run around anywhere allowed by his leash, and his leash can wrap around trees.



Assuming a negligible circumference of the trees, how many trees can the dog reach if his leash must be taut when he reaches the tree?



(Taut means that the leash is not loose; the dog could not go any farther. For example, the dog can reach the tree at $(8,0)$ with his leash taut, but if there were a tree at $(6,0)$, you could not reach it with the leash taut unless, for example, there was another tree at $(7,0)$, and the dog wrapped the leash around that before going back to the tree at $(6,0)$ with the leash taut.)




Problem 7How many $5$-digit numbers contain two pairs of positive digits? i.e. $\pmb{3}0\pmb{3}\pmb{99}$ and $\pmb{8}6\pmb{844}$ work, but $12876$, $11237$, and $90000$ do not. The digits in the pairs must be different, so if a number has $2$ pairs of $0$s, like $2\pmb{0000}$, it doesn't count.




Problem 8A UFO is traveling through space, and a planet is in a perfectly circular orbit around a star, with any given point on the orbit exactly $20,000$ miles away from the star. Currently, the UFO is located on the midpoint of the segment connecting the star and planet. The UFO is traveling in a straight line, and it will collide with the planet when the planet has completed $\frac{1}{3}$ of its orbit. If the ratio of the UFO's speed to the planet's speed can be expressed as $\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c\pi}$, where $a,b$, and $c$ are positive integers, $a$ and $c$ are relatively prime, and $b$ is not divisible by the square of any prime, find the value of $a+b+c$.




Problem 9A bug starts out at the origin of the $2D$ plane. It makes a series of moves where in each move it chooses a lattice point and moves to the lattice point in a line segment, without passing through any other lattice point (for example, it cannot move directly from $(-1,-1)$ to  $(1,1)$). After a series of moves, it has traveled a total of $6$ units and has landed on a lattice point $(x,y)$ satisfying $|x|+|y|=4$. How many possible distinct sequences of moves are possible?




Problem 10Each square of a 6 by 6 grid is colored red or blue. What is the probability that there is an even number of red squares in each row or column? Express your answer as a common fraction.

topics.title: The Frog Riddle
topics.text:
There are two videos I watched. One is about solving the Frog Riddle problem with a solution:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cpwSGsb-rTs



There is another video where a man argues that Ted-Ed is wrong.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=go3xtDdsNQM



Who is right? I am confused of who is right, so I want you guys to give an opinion.

ProblemYou eat a poisonous mushroom, and you are about to die. There is a species of frog that can cure you, but only the female kind will actually cure you. Female and male frogs occur equally, and they look exactly alike, except that males have a distinctive croak.

You see a tree stump, and on the stump lies a frog. However, in the other direction, you hear a croak. You find two frogs in a clearing, and you don't know which frog made the croak. If you go this route, you will lick the frogs together because the male frogs are not poisonous.

Which path should you take and why?




Ted-Ed's ExplanationThe chance of living from the frog on the tree stump is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

You have a sample space of $MM,MF,FM,FF$ for the frogs in the clearing. We have to eliminate $FF$ because we heard a male croak. Now we have $MM,MF,FM$ left. There is now a $\dfrac{2}{3}$ that you will live from the frog clearing, and that is the better option.




MindYourDecisions's ExplanationThe chance of living from the frog on the tree stump is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The detail that you heard a croak changes the problem. Now you have a sample space of $M_0 M_1, M_1 M_0, M_1 F, F M_1$. This then gives you a $\dfrac{1}{2}$ chance of living from the clearing frogs, and an equal chance to live.

topics.title: Is Special Training Needed for MathCounts Countdown Round

Does one need to pick up some special skills/knowledge/tactics to be competitive in the "countdown" round?



For example, it appears obvious that one has to be able to do mental arithmetic quickly and accurately. Unless there is a better way, I think he had to 1) prime factorize, 2) find the sum of the geometric sequence for each prime factor, and 3) multiply all the sums.   I am wondering if he had to go thru special training to get to that speed.



If so, is it worthwhile to train for such skills, which are almost entirely useless later on in life (not even useful for later math contests)?   Would a student be better served to use that time for some real math?



Would love to hear thoughts from anyone, especially those with actual "countdown" round experience.

topics.title: Can anyone give me a clue? HIDE THE ANSWER PLEASE
topics.text:
This problem that I found is confusing. Can anyone give me some clues to solve this problem?



My uncle never learned how to simplify fractions properly. When he sees a fraction like $\dfrac{16}{64}$, he "cancels" the sixes: $\dfrac{1\cancel{6}}{\cancel{6}4}$, yielding $\dfrac{1}{4}$.



Miraculously, this is the right answer! This trick doesn't usually work, though; my uncle just got lucky. For example, you can check that $\dfrac{24}{48}$ is not equal to $\dfrac{2}{8}$. But as they say, even a stopped clock tells the right time twice a day...



There are three other fractions for which my uncle's simplification happens to be correct. In other words, besides $\dfrac{16}{64}$, there are three other fractions of the form $\dfrac{ab}{bc}$ which are equal to $\dfrac{a}{c}$ (where $ab$ and $bc$ represent 2-digit numbers, not products). See if you can find these fractions.

topics.title: They're easier then they look.
topics.text:
a) How many integers $k$ are there such that $\sqrt[n]{k}$ is never able to be simplified for all positive integers $n$ if $n\not=1$?



b) How many composite integers $p$ are there such that $\sqrt[n]{p}$ is never able to be simplified for all positive integers $n$ if $n\not=1$?



c) How many pairs of integers $(a, b)$ are there such that $\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $\sqrt[n]{b}$ are both never able to be simplified for all positive integers $n$ if $\gcd(a, b)=1$ and $n\not=1$?





SolutionsaSince all primes work, and there are infinitely many primesTake a prime $z$, and $z!$.

Thus, $z!$ is divisible by every prime under $z$. And also, $z!+1$ is NOT divisible by every prime under $z$. But what if it is prime? We found a new prime! If it's composite? It's divisible by a prime $r$ that satisfies $r>z$. So, we have a new prime.
 and we have $\boxed{\text{infinite}}$.


bWe can just take any two primes from our infinite mix of primes, and multiply them, which can be done in $\boxed{\text{infinite}}$ ways.


cWe can take any two primes again, from the composite factorization from part b. But now, we just put them in a pair $(a, b)$. Just a different rewording. But remember to answer the question, and it's $\boxed{\text{infinite}}$.
